value_proposition: A full-stack quantum platform centered on high-fidelity, fully connected trapped-ion quantum computers, offered through cloud and on-premises access and supported by optimization software, simulators, SDK integrations, and applications expertise. IonQ positions the platform for practical hybrid workflows today and modular, fault-tolerant logical computation in the future.
target_customers: Enterprises pursuing quantum and hybrid quantum-classical workflows
qubit_modality: Trapped ion qubits using individual ionized ytterbium atoms (Yb+) confined in linear ion traps and prepared, controlled, entangled, and read out using lasers. The roadmap introduces microwave gate operations and an Electronic Qubit Control architecture.
hardware_architecture: Current disclosed architecture uses chains of ytterbium ions in lithographically produced linear ion traps with roughly 100 electrodes, housed in ultra-high-vacuum chambers around 10^-11 Torr. Individual and global laser beams perform gates; fluorescence provides simultaneous readout. Current systems use optical gate operations and acoustic-optic-deflector gate control. Ion chains provide all-to-all connectivity. The future scaling architecture is modular, with 2D arrays, microwave operations, Electronic Qubit Control, and eventually photonic interconnects between modules.
current_systems: IonQ Forte: 36 physical qubits, 99.6% two-qubit-gate fidelity, 99.98% one-qubit-gate fidelity, all-to-all connectivity; described elsewhere as being in limited-access beta

IonQ Forte Enterprise: 36 physical qubits, 99.6% two-qubit-gate fidelity, 99.98% one-qubit-gate fidelity, all-to-all connectivity; rack-mounted and intended for on-premises, production-ready hybrid workflows
IonQ Aria: described as commercially available, but no specifications are supplied
IonQ simulators: noisy simulators and an ideal state simulator
IonQ Harmony: named in the product navigation, but no current specifications or availability details are supplied
physical_qubit_scale: Currently specified Forte and Forte Enterprise systems have 36 physical qubits. IonQ reports single-qubit gates on a 79-ion chain and complex algorithms on chains of 35+ ions; these are demonstrations, not stated commercial-system capacities. A customer case study also references benefits from 46 qubits without identifying the underlying system. Tempo's 100 qubits and all larger figures are future targets, not current capabilities.
one_qubit_fidelity: Current Forte and Forte Enterprise specification: 99.98% one-qubit-gate fidelity. A 99.99% figure appears as a broader world-record/roadmap claim, but it is not identified as the current commercial-system one-qubit specification.
two_qubit_fidelity: Current Forte and Forte Enterprise specification: 99.6% two-qubit-gate fidelity. The homepage separately claims a world-record 99.99% two-qubit-gate fidelity, but the supplied material does not identify the system, test conditions, or whether this is sustained across a commercial QPU.
connectivity: Current Forte and Forte Enterprise systems have all-to-all connectivity. The technology page says every qubit can interact with every other qubit without intermediary routing. Tempo is specified as future many-to-many connectivity, while the broader roadmap targets all-to-all connectivity in later generations.
coherence: The homepage reports T1 and T2 time as '10–100s, ~1s,' apparently indicating a 10–100-second range and approximately 1 second, but it does not unambiguously map each value to T1 or T2 or identify the measured system. The technology page says prepared ytterbium states are long-lived but provides no additional measured coherence benchmark.
error_correction_strategy: No currently demonstrated quantum-error-correction implementation or logical-qubit result is disclosed. Current cloud features include error mitigation, proprietary compilation, circuit optimization, and noisy simulation. The roadmap proposes applying quantum error correction to high-fidelity physical qubits, supplemented by quantum-memory technology, with a target of 12 logical qubits and logical error below 1.00E-7 in 2026.
fault_tolerance_strategy: Future strategy: combine high-fidelity trapped-ion physical qubits, quantum error correction, long-lived quantum memory, modular trapped-ion subsystems, Electronic Qubit Control, 2D arrays, mid-circuit measurement, parallel operations, and later photonic interconnects. No fault-tolerant system is shown as currently demonstrated in the supplied material.
roadmap: Late 2026 Tempo target: 100 physical qubits, 99.9% two-qubit-gate fidelity, 99.99% one-qubit-gate fidelity, and many-to-many connectivity

2026 roadmap target: 100–256+ physical qubits, 99.99% physical-qubit fidelity, 12 logical qubits, logical error below 1.00E-7, microwave gates, 2D arrays, mid-circuit measurement, and parallel operations
2026 next-generation EQC architecture: begin with a 256-qubit system and provide a semiconductor-oriented path toward 10,000 qubits and beyond
2027 target: 10,000 physical qubits and 800 logical qubits with logical error below 1.00E-7
2028 target: 20,000 physical qubits and 1,600 logical qubits with logical error below 1.00E-7
2029 target: 200,000 physical qubits and 8,000 logical qubits, logical error stated as below 1.00^-12, and photonic interconnects
2030 target: 2,000,000 physical qubits and 80,000 logical qubits, logical error stated as below 1.00^-12, and photonic interconnects
IonQ also states a broader 2030 conversion range of 40,000–80,000 logical qubits from more than 2,000,000 physical qubits; this differs from the roadmap's specific 80,000-logical-qubit target
access_methods: Partner-cloud access also advertised for NVIDIA
Noisy simulators and ideal state simulator
Research Credits Program for eligible academics
manufacturing_strategy: Current ion traps use precisely designed and lithographed electrode chips. Future scaling is presented as a modular architecture and an Electronic Qubit Control semiconductor path. The homepage also discusses quantum-grade diamond thin films and foundry-scale semiconductor manufacturing, but the supplied material does not establish that this is the manufacturing process for the current ytterbium trapped-ion QPUs.
software_stack: Proprietary compiler and circuit optimization software
Organization, project, administration, and usage-management tools
commercial_deployments: Forte and Forte Enterprise are presented as accessible QPUs; Forte is also described as limited-access beta
Aria is described as commercially available, without supplied specifications
Forte Enterprise is offered as a rack-mounted on-premises system
IonQ reports commercial-system activity at sites in Washington, DC; Seattle; Toronto; and Basel, but does not identify which are customer deployments

AstraZeneca/AWS/NVIDIA hybrid chemistry work: reported 20x faster time-to-solution than the best previously published implementation; the homepage separately claims at least 656x acceleration for a complex chemistry simulation
Ansys medical-device optimization: reported 12% improvement over classical computing on a problem with more than 2.6 million vertices and 40 million edges
Hyundai road-sign image recognition: an 8-qubit quantum-machine-learning demonstration using fewer input parameters than comparable classical approaches
Industrial materials and AI work: reported 3.14% accuracy improvement and reduced energy use at scale from a 46-qubit hybrid workflow; the customer is not named in the supplied material
strengths: Current commercial systems disclose strong 99.6% two-qubit and 99.98% one-qubit fidelity rather than relying only on qubit count
All-to-all connectivity reduces routing and swap overhead for current systems
Long-lived atomic qubits and ultra-high-vacuum isolation provide a strong physical basis for stable computation
Broad access model spanning direct cloud, major public clouds, on-demand use, reservations, simulators, and on-premises deployment
Extensive SDK compatibility lowers developer lock-in and integration effort
Multiple disclosed enterprise-oriented hybrid demonstrations across chemistry, engineering, automotive, materials, and AI
Modular scaling and photonic interconnect plans directly address the limits of monolithic ion chains
Enterprise features include organization management, dashboards, usage reporting, support, and system-status monitoring
weaknesses: Current specified commercial scale is only 36 physical qubits, while useful fault-tolerant computation remains a roadmap objective
No currently demonstrated logical qubit count or logical error rate is supplied
The claimed 99.99% two-qubit world record is not reconciled with the 99.6% specification of Forte and Forte Enterprise
Forte is described as limited-access beta, indicating access or product maturity constraints
No gate-duration or throughput benchmark is supplied, limiting time-to-solution comparison at the hardware level
Coherence information is ambiguously formatted and is not tied to a named system or measurement protocol
Several application claims lack enough methodological detail in the supplied pages to independently assess classical baselines, workload boundaries, or the quantum hardware's exact contribution
The roadmap requires an exceptionally large scale-up from tens or hundreds of physical qubits to 10,000 in 2027 and 2 million in 2030
competitive_differentiators: Natural, identical ytterbium atomic qubits rather than fabricated synthetic qubits
All-to-all interaction within current ion chains
Room-temperature supporting hardware, despite laser cooling of the ions
Software-configurable and on-demand ion-chain sizing without fabricating a new trap for each qubit count
Combination of cloud access, multi-cloud integrations, direct access, and rack-mounted on-premises systems
Native support for a broad range of third-party SDKs and libraries
Future modular trapped-ion strategy combining Electronic Qubit Control, quantum memory, and photonic interconnects
Emphasis on application-level metrics such as solution quality and time-to-solution rather than physical-qubit count alone
technical_risks: Scaling from 36-qubit commercial systems to thousands or millions of physical qubits requires major advances in control electronics, traps, optical or microwave control, packaging, calibration, and interconnects
Maintaining current fidelity and connectivity while moving from 1D optical-control systems to 2D microwave/EQC architectures is not demonstrated in the supplied material
The roadmap's logical-qubit and logical-error targets depend on an undisclosed error-correcting code, resource model, and experimentally validated fault-tolerance stack
Photonic interconnects are not planned until 2029 in the stated roadmap, creating dependence on later-stage networking technology for the largest systems
Longer ion chains can face increased control complexity and collective-motion challenges; the supplied material shows complex algorithms only on 35+ ion chains
Ultra-high-vacuum operation and precision laser, optical, mechanical, and firmware control create substantial systems-engineering and reliability requirements
The architecture's gate speed is undisclosed, so high fidelity and connectivity may not necessarily translate into superior workload throughput
Roadmap notation for logical error rates ('1.00^-12') is unclear, reducing technical interpretability
commercialization_risks: The commercial value proposition depends heavily on roadmap achievements that are far beyond the currently specified 36-qubit systems
Limited-access status for Forte may constrain customer experimentation and revenue scalability
On-premises trapped-ion systems may require specialized installation, calibration, maintenance, vacuum, and precision-control support
Strong application claims may be difficult for buyers to evaluate without fuller disclosure of baselines, costs, runtimes, hardware configurations, and reproducibility details
Large-scale fault-tolerant systems depend on delivering multiple new technologies on aggressive annual timelines
The supplied material does not disclose pricing for direct QPU access or on-premises systems, apart from volume-based and custom-pricing language

Inconsistent figures—such as 99.99% record fidelity versus 99.6% commercial specification, 40,000–80,000 versus 80,000 logical qubits, and 20x versus 656x chemistry acceleration—may create buyer confusion
The 46-qubit application claim is not reconciled with the 36-qubit specifications of the named current systems
marketing_message: IonQ presents itself as the only full-stack quantum platform and the leader in high-fidelity trapped-ion computing, offering enterprise-accessible quantum systems and practical hybrid results today while pursuing the fastest modular path to millions of physical qubits and tens of thousands of fault-tolerant logical qubits by 2030.

The relationship between current optical-control systems and future microwave/EQC systems is not explained in enough detail to assess transition risk
